story: A September 18th paper in Communications Earth and Environment shows Indigenous observations from coastal Arctic Alaska caught an Arctic Ocean model error that conventional metrics miss, with AAOKH observers as co-authors
transcription_note: Quoted passages in the verbatim fields are transcribed to plain ASCII, because this record publishes into a house style that bans em and en dashes and curly quotes. Three kinds of change were made and none alters a word. En dashes in ranges and in model names are written out (the source prints 1993-2023 and MOM6-COBALT-ARC11k with en dashes). Utqiagvik is written without the dot above the g that the paper uses. Inupiat is written without the n tilde that the University of Alaska release uses. Where a transcription was made, the claim's own notes field says so. For the exact printed characters, read the source at the claim's source_url.

claims.claim: The paper "Indigenous Knowledge and observations improve Arctic Ocean model skill and relevance" was published online on September 18th in Communications Earth and Environment.
claims.verbatim: Published Date: September 18, 2026 (published-online)
claims.notes: Publisher-deposited metadata. The journal's formal name uses an ampersand. The UAF release calls it Nature Communications Earth and Environment, which is the release being loose; the journal's own name wins.

claims.claim: The paper carries DOI 10.1038/s43247-026-03899-w and is article 748 in volume 7 of the journal.
claims.verbatim: Volume 7, Issue 1, Article 748
claims.notes: DOI resolves to the article page, which returned full text.

claims.claim: The paper has ten authors, listed in order as Claudine Hauri, Donna D. W. Hauser, Billy Adams, Victoria Q. Buschman, Roberta T. Glenn, Krista Heeringa, Brita Irving, Joseph M. Leavitt, Remi Pages and Robert Schaeffer.
claims.verbatim: Claudine Hauri, Donna D. W. Hauser, Billy Adams, Victoria Q. Buschman, Roberta T. Glenn, Krista Heeringa, Brita Irving, Joseph M. Leavitt, Remi Pages, Robert Schaeffer
claims.notes: Confirmed independently against the article page. The scouts' partial list omitted Buschman, Heeringa, Irving and Pages. The deck must not imply a six-author paper.

claims.claim: Lead author Claudine Hauri is a research faculty member at the International Arctic Research Center at the University of Alaska Fairbanks.
claims.verbatim: Claudine Hauri, research faculty member at IARC
claims.notes: Rests on UAF's own release, not on the paper. The paper's affiliations block was unreachable through three routes, so affiliations for the other nine authors are NOT verified and must not be asserted.

claims.claim: The Alaska Arctic Observatory and Knowledge Hub database holds over 12,000 observation records.
claims.verbatim: The AAOKH database contains over 12,000 records from across >1500 km of coastline, documenting sea ice, ocean conditions, weather, fish and marine wildlife, and unusual or extreme events.
claims.notes: Retrieved identically through two independent routes. The paper says over 12,000, not a precise count, so write it as over 12,000 and never as exactly 12,000.

claims.claim: Those AAOKH records come from more than 1,500 kilometres of Arctic Alaska coastline.
claims.verbatim: over 12,000 records from across >1500 km of coastline
claims.notes: Measures the extent of coastline the records span, not a survey line or a model domain.

claims.claim: AAOKH observers record sea ice, ocean conditions, weather, fish and marine wildlife, and unusual or extreme events.
claims.verbatim: documenting sea ice, ocean conditions, weather, fish and marine wildlife, and unusual or extreme events
claims.notes: The paper's own list. It does not say harvest here; do not add harvest to this list.

claims.claim: AAOKH and its predecessor the Seasonal Ice Zone Observing Network have sustained knowledge exchange with Indigenous environmental observers in coastal Arctic Alaska since 2006.
claims.verbatim: Since 2006, AAOKH and its predecessor program (Seasonal Ice Zone Observing Network, SIZONet) have nurtured sustained knowledge exchange between researchers and a network of Indigenous environmental observers in coastal Arctic Alaska.
claims.notes: 2006 is the start of the combined SIZONet plus AAOKH lineage, not the founding date of AAOKH itself. A slide saying AAOKH has run since 2006 would misstate the paper.

claims.claim: The model is the MOM6 COBALT ARC11k configuration, built on the Modular Ocean Model version 6, the Sea Ice Simulator version 2 and the COBALT version 3 biogeochemical model.
claims.verbatim: based on the Modular Ocean Model version 6 (MOM6), the Sea Ice Simulator version 2 (SIS2), and the Carbon, Ocean Biogeochemistry, and Lower Trophics version 3 (COBALTv3) biogeochemical model.
claims.notes: Confirms the coupling of ocean, sea ice and biogeochemistry. The paper's own string uses en dashes between the three components; house style bans them, so write MOM6 COBALT ARC11k on slides.

claims.claim: The analysis used a regional Arctic Ocean hindcast simulation covering 1993 to 2023.
claims.verbatim: a regional Arctic Ocean hindcast simulation
claims.notes: Hindcast, not forecast. A 31 year span. The word hindcast is the paper's own. The printed range uses an en dash in the source; written here as 1993 to 2023 per house style.

claims.claim: Model output was spatially averaged over an area of roughly 4,100 square kilometres around Utqiagvik.
claims.verbatim: spatially averaged around Utqiagvik (~4100 km2)
claims.notes: Only one scout reported this, so it was checked twice and survived through both routes. It is the averaging area for model output around Utqiagvik, NOT the study area, NOT AAOKH's coverage, and NOT the model domain. Label it precisely.

claims.claim: In 2019, during a major marine heatwave, the model predicted sea ice would freeze up earlier than it actually did.
claims.verbatim: In 2019, during a major marine heatwave, the model predicted sea ice would freeze up earlier than it actually did.
claims.notes: The load-bearing sentence of the deck. Direction confirmed verbatim through three separate fetches. The model froze the ice too EARLY; reality froze LATE. The paper gives NO quantification of the gap, so the deck can't print a magnitude.

claims.claim: Indigenous observers in that season reported late freeze up, warm conditions and stormy weather, which made hunting especially difficult.
claims.verbatim: Indigenous observers reported late freeze-up, warm conditions, and stormy weather, which made hunting especially difficult.
claims.notes: The observed side of the C12 discrepancy, in the paper's words.

claims.claim: The paper states that Indigenous Knowledge can identify model deficiencies that conventional metrics miss.
claims.verbatim: demonstrating how Indigenous Knowledge can identify model deficiencies that conventional metrics miss
claims.notes: The paper says conventional metrics MISS, not that they would not have caught it, which is a stronger counterfactual. Attribute as the authors' argument, not as established fact.

claims.claim: The paper states that Indigenous Knowledge does not require validation by scientific frameworks.
claims.verbatim: Indigenous Knowledge does not require validation by scientific frameworks.
claims.notes: Verified verbatim through two routes. The authors' position statement. Present with attribution, never as the deck's own editorial voice.

claims.claim: The paper states that Indigenous observers are co-authors of the work and shape its research questions, the interpretation of model results and the priorities for model development.
claims.verbatim: Indigenous observers are co-authors of this work and actively shape the research questions, the interpretation of model results, and the priorities for model development.
claims.notes: The strongest support for the deck's thesis. It says Indigenous observers are co-authors WITHOUT naming which of the ten, and the affiliations block is unreachable, so the deck must NOT name any individual as Indigenous on the strength of this.

claims.claim: The paper reports the model generally captured the timing of seasonal changes, especially the end of the open water season.
claims.verbatim: we found the model generally captured the timing of seasonal changes, especially the end of the open-water season
claims.notes: The fairness claim, and it belongs on a slide. The finding is not that the model was bad. It is that the model was broadly right and the observers found the specific place it was wrong. A deck that prints C12 without C17 is a takedown and is not what the paper says.

claims.claim: In Utqiagvik the fall 2019 bowhead whale hunt yielded only one whale, against historical fall harvests of up to about 30.
claims.verbatim: with only one whale harvested compared to historical fall harvests of up to ~30 whales
claims.notes: The ~30 is the paper's approximation of a historical upper bound, not an average, so write up to about 30 and never normally 30. Fall harvest only; the spring hunt is a separate season and must not be blended in.

claims.claim: The modeling work sits within the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's Changing Ecosystems and Fisheries Initiative.
claims.verbatim: as part of the U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's (NOAA) Changing Ecosystems and Fisheries Initiative (CEFI)
claims.notes: The paper also describes CEFI as a U.S. program developing an operational modeling and decision-support system. Do not claim CEFI funded or endorsed the paper.

claims.claim: The paper used a seasonal calendar for Utqiagvik as the shared format for putting Indigenous observations and model output side by side.
claims.verbatim: To show how Indigenous observations and Arctic Ocean model output can work together, we used a seasonal calendar for Utqiagvik, Alaska.
claims.notes: The paper covered two calendar years, September 2018 to August 2019 and September 2019 to August 2020. The scouts' phrase interwoven seasonal calendars is NOT the paper's and must not be quoted as such.

claims.claim: The paper describes seasonal calendars as reflecting the cycles of the seasons and the close connections between environmental conditions and community harvesting activities.
claims.verbatim: Seasonal calendars reflect the cycles of the seasons and the close connections between environmental conditions and community harvesting activities, making them a locally meaningful format for dialogue.
claims.notes: The paper's definition of the device.

claims.claim: The paper argues that academic institutions reward productivity, publications and novelty, while co-production requires patience and a pace set by relationship rather than deadlines.
claims.verbatim: Academic institutions reward productivity, publications, and novelty. Co-production requires patience and adaptability to let community priorities redirect research questions and the willingness to work at a pace determined by relationship rather than deadlines.
claims.notes: The paper adds that co-production risks becoming a box to check rather than a genuine commitment, which is the sharper pull quote. Attribute to the authors.

claims.claim: The paper reports that AAOKH observer stipends were historically supported by longer term funding but that stability is no longer guaranteed, and sustaining them has become a project by project effort.
claims.verbatim: AAOKH observer stipends have historically been supported by longer-term funding mechanisms, but that stability is no longer guaranteed, and sustaining them has increasingly become a project-by-project effort.
claims.notes: Specific rather than general grievance. The paper does not name a cancelled program or a dollar figure, so the deck must not supply one.

claims.claim: The published funding record for the paper names NOAA awards NA24OARX431C and NA23OAR4690390, Office of Naval Research award N00014-22-1-2792, and the Sasakawa Peace Foundation.
claims.verbatim: National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (Awards: NA24OARX431C, NA23OAR4690390) - Office of Naval Research (Award: N00014-22-1-2792) - Sasakawa Peace Foundation
claims.notes: The structured funder deposit, not the paper's prose Acknowledgements, which was unreachable. If the deck prints funders, hedge with the published funding record lists.

claims.claim: Utqiagvik observer Billy Adams recorded on October 1st, 2019 that it had rained so much the roads were falling apart and a temperature record might have been broken.
claims.verbatim: It has rained so much that the roads are falling apart and we may have broken a temperature record. Everyone is waiting for snow. The bowhead whales are not close to Barrow yet either. Feels like many natural cycles the animals go through normally are being changed and the minds are being tested.
claims.notes: Verbatim and untruncated. An observation record from the exact season the model got wrong, in the observer's own voice. The date carries a different calendar year so the year stays per house rule. The release uses Barrow inside the quote, which is the observer's own word and must not be silently changed.

claims.claim: Billy Adams said he thinks it is going to be a big thing very soon to have Indigenous input in ice and ocean modeling.
claims.verbatim: I think it's going to be a big thing very soon to have Indigenous input in ice and ocean modeling, and with all fairness to the animals that we depend on, is looking for the truth of how our populations are doing in the marine environment.
claims.notes: Adams is a named co-author and the release identifies him as an observer in Utqiagvik. Quote with attribution to the UAF release, not to the paper.

claims.claim: Claudine Hauri said the observations are not just data points, because an Inupiat observer noticing something about the sea ice is drawing on generations of knowledge about how that ice behaves.
claims.verbatim: These aren't just data points. When an Inupiat observer notices something about the sea ice, they're drawing on generations of knowledge about how that ice behaves, what it means for travel and hunting, and how it connects to wind, currents and animals.
claims.notes: Verbatim and untruncated. The full quote continues that this is a different kind of knowing than a single measurement. The release spells it with the n tilde.

claims.claim: Claudine Hauri said the partnership fundamentally changed the way the team conducts research, and that the model framework was co-developed with Indigenous observers.
claims.verbatim: This partnership fundamentally changed the way we conduct research. Instead of simply applying scientific questions to data, we co-developed the model framework with Indigenous observers, centering the research around community needs and priorities.
claims.notes: A one-sided framing by definition, the lead author describing her own project in her institution's release. Attribute plainly to Hauri and do not let it carry a factual assertion on its own.

claims.claim: AAOKH works with northern Alaska coastal communities including Tikigaq, Kotzebue, Wainwright, Utqiagvik and Kaktovik.
claims.verbatim: helps northern Alaska coastal communities share their expertise and observations of changing sea ice, wildlife and coastal waters
claims.source_outlet: International Arctic Research Center, University of Alaska Fairbanks
claims.notes: Fetched on the run date after aaokh.org failed DNS. An undated program page, so the community list should be read as current rather than as the roster at any particular time. The paper separately credits a Figure 1 photo to Guy Omnik from Tikigaq, which corroborates Tikigaq's involvement.
